ops.text: To hold specific metal ions in a stable and energetically favorable manner, metalloproteins across all species have evolved topologically similar metal-binding sites in their structures to meet the chemical and geometric bonding requirements 3 . Over the decades, both structural observations and theoretical calculations have accumulated detailed knowledge to accurately describe the rules of binding geometry and valence for different metal ions 4 . More recently, researchers have explored metal-binding proteins directly in proteomes using other experimental methods including inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) 5 , activity-based protein profiling 6 and metal isotope native radio autography in gel electrophoresis 7 .

ops.text: We applied MetalNet to predict metalloproteins in four prokaryotic proteomes, including Escherichia coli, Bacillus subtilis, Saccharolobus solfataricus and Halobacterium salinarum, which currently have 1,965 annotated metalloproteins. MetalNet predicted a total of 4,849 potential metalloproteins in these species (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Dataset 4). Moreover, MetalNet found 1,603 network clusters and we were able to match the co-evolution network patterns for 973 of them so that their metal types could be inferred by analogy to existing metalloproteins (Supplementary Dataset 4).

ops.text: We first sought direct structural evidence to support our predictions. For each of the predicted metalloproteins, we searched its homologs by PDB-BLAST 33 and found that 37% (1,810 of 4,849) of the predictions could be supported by experimental structures (Fig. 3b ). Among these predictions, we not only observed classical short sequence motifs such as C2H2 in zinc fingers and CXXCXXCC in certain iron-sulfur-binding proteins but also found cases with metal-chelating residues by >100 amino acids apart in sequence (Fig. 3c ) or with complexed co-evolved networks corresponding to multinuclear or multiple metal-binding sites (Fig. 3d , e ). Collectively, these examples highlighted the power of MetalNet in discovering complex metal-binding sites from proteins independent from 1D sequences or 3D structural motifs.

ops.text: Fig. 2 | Assembly of metal-binding residue pairs into a high-order connected co-evolution network by graph theory. Co-evolved metal-binding residue pairs predicted by ML model are assembled into a high-order co-evolution network, and the connected sub-networks are then detected by graph theory. The 'singleton' pairs are discarded, which can serve as a filter to increase the prediction precision. Finally, the predicted sub-network clusters are queried in a 'co-evolution motif bank' compiled from known metalloproteins (histidine in blue, cysteine in yellow, aspartic acid in purple and glutamic acid in pink), which will enable prediction of the type of metal ions bound. It should be noted that one metal type might have multiple corresponding network motifs in the bank.

ops.text: We next investigated whether evolutionary information extracted from metagenome sequencing data can enhance MetalNet predictions. We started with the MSAs that were previously calculated by GREMLIN to guide the structural modeling of 1,116 Pfam families by Rosetta (ref. 22 ). MetalNet predicted 175 metalloproteins with clusters and 60 of them have overlapping Rosetta models (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Dataset 5). Analysis of these models showed that residues within 46 predicted metal-binding sites are proximal to each other (Supplementary Dataset 5 and Supplementary Fig. 1 ). Furthermore, the overall distribution of residue-residue distances was consistent with that calculated from known metalloproteins below 4.5 Å (Extended Data Fig. 7 ).

ops.text: We selected 21 MetalNet predictions for experimental validation, none of which has been reported with any metal-binding activities or homologs back then at that time. Five targets yielded reasonable expression in the initial screening including Rv3033, Desor_0198, SVEN_5263, cbrC and citX. Among them, Rv3033 (Uniprot code: I6YAY5 ) failed to be purified likely because it is predicted as an iron-sulfur cluster-binding protein. Purified Desor_0198 (UniProt code: G7W7J8 ) and SVEN_5263 (UniProt code: F2R5E5 ) showed zinc-binding signals by ICP-MS (Extended Data Fig. 8a , b ); however, their metal-binding site variants were unstable for purification. We therefore characterized the remaining two proteins, cbrC and citX, in detail by biochemical and/or structural methods.

ops.text: The protein cbrC (UniProt code: P31469, Pfam: PF03691) is a CreB-regulated gene C protein in E. coli 34 . MetalNet predicted two potential metal-binding sites (Site 1: C31, C33, C34, C56 and C59; Site 2: H125, C126, C182 and C185) (Extended Data Fig. 8c ). We purified the wild-type protein, the single variant of C56S or C182S, as well as the double variant (Extended Data Fig. 8c ). ICP-MS analysis showed that the wild-type protein was bound with zinc and the measured metal to protein ratio was close to two, which is highly consistent with the MetalNet prediction. The zinc/protein ratios of the single variants, C56S and C182S, were measured as 0.481 and 0.628, respectively, and for the double variant of C56S/C182S, its metal-binding activity was completely abolished (Extended Data Fig. 8c ). The protein citX (UniProt code: P0A6G5, Pfam: PF03802) was annotated as an apo-citrate lyase phosphoribosyl-dephospho-CoA transferase in E. coli 35 . MetalNet identified a co-evolution network consisting of three cysteines (C145, C148 and C155) and one histidine H161 in citX (Fig. 4b ), and the network topology confidently matches a zinc-binding site. We recombinantly overexpressed the wild-type citX and the single variants of the four metal-binding residues (C145S, C148S, C155S and H161S) in E. coli, and some of the single variants showed compromised solubility (Fig. 4c ). After purification (Extended Data Fig. 8d ), ICP-MS analysis confirmed that the wild-type protein specifically bound zinc but not iron or copper as expected from the prediction, and the measured metal to protein ratio was around 0.7 and none of the single variants showed detectable zinc-binding signals (Fig. 4d ). When the wild-type protein was treated with EDTA, a conventional metal-chelator, the thermal stability curve was shifted left compared with the sample treated with PBS, indicating the protein was destabilized upon metal extraction (Fig. 4e ). Circular dichroism analysis also showed that EDTA treatment would greatly perturb the protein's conformation (Fig. 4f ). Finally, we solved the structure of citX by X-ray crystallography (PDB code: 7DCM at 2.5 Å resolution determined by single-wavelength anomalous diffraction and PDB code: 7DCN at 1.7 Å resolution determined by molecular replacement; Supplementary Table 3 ). In the structure of 7DCN, distances between the zinc ion and the predicted chelating residues are 2.34 Å, 2.31 Å, 2.36 Å and 2.08 Å, which unambiguously proved that the predicted cysteines and histidine together form a tetrahedral zinc-binding site in citX (Fig. 4g ). The crystal structure also matches well with a structural model we built by Rosetta (Fig. 4h ). To investigate structural and dynamic characteristics of citX and its variants, we also performed molecular dynamic (MD) simulations and the results showed that all the four variants had greater conformational fluctuations at the zinc-binding site, suggesting that the metal ion has a stabilizing effect for the protein (Extended Data Fig. 9 ).

ops.text: We used AutoGluon ( https://auto.gluon.ai/stable/index.html ) to train a high-performance model. AutoGluon is an auto-machine-learning (AutoML) framework, which is developed by researchers in Amazon. Unlike existing AutoML frameworks that primarily focus on model/hyperparameter selection, AutoGluon-Tabular succeeds by ensembling multiple models, including XGBoost, Random Forest model, KNearestNeighbors model, neural network models and so on, and then stacking them in multiple layers. AutoGluon requires only a single line of Python to train highly accurate ML models on an unprocessed tabular dataset. The key parameters are shown as follows: time_limit = 600, metric = 'roc_auc', predictor = TabularPredictor(label = label, eval_metric = metric, verbosity = 0).fit(train_data, time_limit = time_limit, presets = 'best_quality').

ops.text: The protein crystals were picked by cryo-loops and placed in the corresponding reservoir solution, containing 20% (vol/vol) glycerol and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The X-ray data were collected at Beamline 17U1 and BL19U of Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility at the Se peak wavelength 0.9792 Å with Eiger 16 M detector, and the samples were kept at 100 K during data collection. The initial model was determined by single-wavelength anomalous diffraction phasing using the anomalous signal from Se atoms with SHELX 53 using the peak data and finally refined to a resolution of 2.5 Å. Model building and refinement were carried out iteratively using Phenix 54 and Coot 55 . Then another higher-resolution structure was determined by molecular replacement with Phenix AutoMR using the initial model as the search model and finally refined to a resolution of 1.7 Å. Final structures were validated with the wwPDB server. The data processing and refinement statistics are summarized in Supplementary Table 3 (from coot).

node.label: Extended Data Fig. 5 |
node.text: Extended Data Fig. 5 | Overall workflow of MetalNet. Starting with the information from coevolution analysis, MetalNet uses a machine learning (ML)-based classifier that has been trained by a benchmark of known metalloproteins to predict whether an individual CHED coevolved residue pair is metal-binding or not. It then employs a graph-based approach to identify high-order coevolution network clusters formed by these coevolved CHED pairs to generate reliable predictions of metal-binding sites in the query protein. In certain cases when the coevolution network topology can be matched to that of known metal-binding sites, the method can also infer the information on the type of metal bound in the predicted site. The method does not use any sequence (1D) or structural (3D) homology information to make predictions.

ops.text: To systematically formulate this approach, we generated a 'pairwise frequency matrix' for every CHED co-evolved residue pair in the contact map. The 21 × 21 matrix is calculated based on the residue-residue frequency profile observed in the homologous sequences for this given pair (20 amino acids and one more position gap). We averaged the matrices for all the metal-binding and nonbinding residue pairs, respectively, and observed very distinct patterns between them (Fig. 1d ). For example, the metal-binding pairs have much more enriched signals in the CHED region whereas signals for the nonbinding pairs are dispersed throughout the whole matrix. We reasoned that such pattern differences can be transformed into a classification problem that is addressable by ML.

ops.text: During investigating the co-evolution network of proteins in the benchmark, we observed that many metal-binding co-evolved pairs assemble to form an integrated network (Extended Data Fig. 2 ). This is consistent with a previous report that residues within a functional site have the tendency to cluster together in a co-evolution network 29 . To quantify whether metal-binding residues are more frequently engaged in a connected co-evolution network, we calculated the number of co-evolved connections ('node degree') for every CHED residue. The results showed that the metal-binding residues indeed have higher node degrees on average than the nonbinding ones (Extended Data Fig. 3 ). We reasoned that detecting such networks should help improve the precision of our prediction (Fig. 2 ). We therefore implemented a graph-based approach to detect co-evolution network clusters from the predicted metal-binding residue pairs by trimming off those 'singleton' pairs (Methods). As expected, applying the graph filter resulted in an improved F1 score of the prediction (Supplementary Table 2 ).

node.text: In light of the explosive growth of genome databases, various bioinformatic methods have also been developed to predict metal-binding sites based on the sequence or/and structural information. For example, zinc-binding proteins in human proteome have been systematically predicted by a combination of sequence and structural homology to known metalloproteins 8 . More sophisticated algorithms such as support vector machines and neural networks were used to identify cysteines and histidines in transition-metal-binding sites from protein primary sequences [9] [10] [11] . Moreover, knowledge of canonical chelating geometries could also be utilized to predict metal-binding sites from apoprotein structures 12 . Lastly, web servers such as MIB 13 and COFACTOR 14 have been developed to enable automated annotation for metal-binding sites or ligand-binding sites in proteins 14 . However, it still remains challenging to computationally discover new classes of metalloproteins without sequence or structural homology in proteomes 3 .

node.text: Thanks to high-throughput sequencing technologies, we are now having access to genome information for a rapidly growing list of species. Alignment of sequences for a given protein of interest (POI) from multiple species enables the construction of its comprehensive evolution history, containing not only highly conserved residues but also pairs of residues with strong covariances. Such co-evolution information, which is often represented in the so-called 'contact map', has been extracted for precise detection of long-range interactions in sequence [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] . More recently, co-evolution signals were harnessed to enable landmark successes in structural predictions for globular proteins [21] [22] [23] , protein complexes 24, 25 and structured states of disordered regions 26 . Co-evolution analyses have also been implemented to define functional sites in proteins in several approaches [27] [28] [29] [30] ; however, its use for systematic prediction of metal-binding sites has not been explored.

node.text: Here we have developed a machine-learning (ML) method named 'MetalNet' to predict metal-binding proteins in proteomes with site-specific resolution using co-evolution. We applied MetalNet to several representative prokaryotic proteomes and predicted nearly 5,000 potential metalloproteins. We biochemically and structurally validated several MetalNet predictions that were previously unannotated, including one zinc-binding site from the apo-citrate lyase phosphoribosyl-dephospho-CoA transferase citX. In addition, MetalNet also successfully predicted all known zinc-binding sites from the human spliceosome complex. This unique computational pipeline will provide a useful tool for exploring unknown metalloproteomes and studying metal biology.

node.text: We first collected metalloproteins from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and crosschecked with the sequence culling database PISCES 31 to get a list of metalloproteins 32 . We also extracted the contact maps for these proteins using the MSA-transformer model (Methods). Classification of the metal-chelating residues showed that cysteine (C), histidine (H), glutamic acid (E) and aspartic acid (D) (together referred as 'CHED') appear much more frequently in metal-binding sites, accounting for 91% of all the metal-chelating residues (Fig. 1a ). For simplicity, we focused only on these four types of amino acids as potential metal-binding residues for following analyses.

node.text: We next analyzed co-evolution signals from all the ten possible pairwise combinations from CHED and observed that many of them showed enriched co-evolution signals compared to those pairs randomly picked from proteomes (Fig. 1b ). For example, 53% of the co-evolved CC residue pairs are involved in metal binding (Fig. 1b ), which is tenfold more enriched than a random CC pair if considering that only 23% of the cysteines in proteomes are chelating metals (Fig. 1c ).

node.text: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to calculate root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) for citX (PDB code: 7DCN ) and its variants. We utilized the GROMACS 2019.3 package and its analytical tools 56 . 'Mutagenesis' tool within PyMOL 57 was used for constructing the citX variants. Each system was solvated in a cubic box filled with TIP3P water model and neutralized by Na + ions. Each system was then minimized and two equilibration steps were set up under constant temperate (NVT) and constant pressure (NPT) for 0.1 ns, respectively. For production runs, the temperature was coupled with V-rescale method and the pressure was coupled with the Parrinello-Rahman method 58 . The Particle Mesh Ewald method was used for calculation of long-range electrostatics 59 . Each system was simulated for 40 ns and the last 10 ns trajectory was used for RMSF calculation.
